## 👀 Mission Background
Next week we start building models. Before anyone does that, the grant program director wants to *see* the data: what each variable looks like, how variables move together, and whether anything is hiding underneath.

Today every section answers one question with the right chart.

* ✅ **Already written:** code you know from Labs 1 to 4. Run it, then answer the question.
* 🆕 **Code with me:** new code. We write it together.

**Your Goal:** Run the second half of the EDA checklist (steps 6 to 9), and leave with a toolbox of charts you can use on any dataset.

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# --- UTILITY REFERENCE ---
# readr, dplyr, tidyr: loading and shaping data (Labs 1 to 4).
# ggplot2: every chart in this lab.
# ggridges: 🆕 ridgeline charts.
# GGally: 🆕 scatterplot matrices.
# plotly: 🆕 interactive charts you can hover over.
# maps: 🆕 US state outlines for maps.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggridges)
library(GGally)
library(plotly)
library(maps)

climate_path <- file.path("../../data", "climate_stations_clean_lon_lat.csv")
grants_path  <- file.path("../../data", "resilience_grants_clean.csv")
```

---

## 0. ✅ Setup: Build the Two Tables (already written for you)
This chunk loads both clean files and builds the two tables you'll use all lab. You've seen every function in it before. Run it as is.

```{r load-and-build, message=FALSE}
climate <- read_csv(climate_path) %>%
  mutate(year = as.numeric(format(reading_date, "%Y")))

grants <- read_csv(grants_path)

# Table 1: one row per station per year, labeled Funded / Not funded (same as Lab 4)
grants_per_year <- grants %>%
  count(location, award_year, name = "n_grants")

station_years <- climate %>%
  left_join(grants_per_year, by = c("location", "year" = "award_year")) %>%
  mutate(
    n_grants = coalesce(n_grants, 0L),
    funded = if_else(n_grants > 0, "Funded", "Not funded")
  )

# Table 2: one row per town, with its weather and its grant totals
town_funding <- grants %>%
  group_by(location) %>%
  summarize(
    total_grants = sum(amount_usd),
    n_grants = n()
  )

towns <- climate %>%
  group_by(location, latitude, longitude) %>%
  summarize(
    avg_rain = mean(precipitation_mm),
    avg_temp = mean(temp_c),
    avg_co2 = mean(co2_ppm),
    storms = sum(extreme_weather_events),
    # the risk level the town had most often across its 7 years
    risk_level = names(which.max(table(climate_risk_level))),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  left_join(town_funding, by = "location") %>%
  mutate(
    total_grants = coalesce(total_grants, 0),
    grants_millions = total_grants / 1e6,
    n_grants = coalesce(n_grants, 0L),
    risk_level = factor(risk_level, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))
  )

glimpse(station_years)
glimpse(towns)
```

**Question 0.1:** How many rows does each table have? In plain words, what does one row represent in each?

# ✅ Checkpoint 1: Seeing Shapes

## 1. ✅ The Boxplot That Hides a Secret
**functions:**
`geom_boxplot()`: Median, middle 50%, and spread (Lab 4).
`geom_histogram()`: The full shape (Lab 2).

**logic steps:**
Draw a boxplot of `temp_c`, then a histogram of the same column.

```{r}
ggplot(station_years, aes(x = "", y = temp_c)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#274873", alpha = 0.5, width = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Temperature: Boxplot", x = NULL, y = "Temperature (°C)") +
  theme_minimal()

ggplot(station_years, aes(x = temp_c)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#274873", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Temperature: Histogram", x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 1.1:** What does the histogram show that the boxplot can't? Why can't a boxplot show it?

---

## 2. 🆕 Violin: Shape Across Groups
**functions:**
`geom_violin()`: 🆕 A density curve mirrored on both sides, one per group.
`reorder(group, value, FUN = median)`: 🆕 Sorts the groups by their median instead of alphabetically.
`scale_fill_viridis_d()`: 🆕 A colorblind-safe palette for categories.

**logic steps:**
Put `energy_source` on the x-axis, sorted by median temperature, and `temp_c` on the y-axis.
Fill each violin by `energy_source`. Hide the legend, since the x-axis already names each group.
Give the chart a title that states the takeaway, and axis labels with units.

```{r}
ggplot(station_years, aes(
  x = reorder(energy_source, temp_c, FUN = median),
  y = temp_c,
  fill = energy_source
)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Solar stations run far hotter than the rest",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 2.1:** Which energy source is the second hump you saw in Section 1? How can you tell?

## 3. 🆕 Ridgeline: Same Question, Another View
**functions:**
`geom_density_ridges()`: 🆕 Stacked density curves, one row per group (from `ggridges`).

**logic steps:**
This time temperature goes on the x-axis and `energy_source` on the y-axis, again sorted by median.
Fill each ridge by `energy_source` and hide the legend.

```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot(station_years, aes(
  x = temp_c,
  y = reorder(energy_source, temp_c, FUN = median),
  fill = energy_source
)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Temperature by Energy Source",
    x = "Temperature (°C)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 3.1:** Violin or ridgeline: which one would you put in a report for the grant director, and why?

## 4. Rare Groups: Fix the Bar Chart

### 4.1 ✅ The Starting Chart
**functions:**
`count()`, `reorder()`, `geom_col()`, `coord_flip()`: Sorted horizontal bar chart (Lab 3).

```{r}
grants %>%
  count(program) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(program, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#274873") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Grants by Program", x = NULL, y = "Number of grants") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 4.1:** Which programs are rare? Roughly what share of all grants does each one have?

### 4.2 🆕 Combine the Rare Programs
**functions:**
`case_when()`: Recodes values by condition (Lab 2).
`%in%`: Checks whether a value is in a list (Lab 1).

**logic steps:**
Create `program_group`: put Drought Response, Heat Resilience, and Wildfire Mitigation together as `"Heat, Drought & Fire"`. Leave every other program as it is.
Count `program_group` and re-draw the sorted bar chart.

```{r}
grants %>%
  mutate(program_group = case_when(
    program %in% c("Drought Response", "Heat Resilience", "Wildfire Mitigation") ~ "Heat, Drought & Fire",
    TRUE ~ program
  )) %>%
  count(program_group) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(program_group, n), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#274873") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Grants by Program (rare programs combined)", x = NULL, y = "Number of grants") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 4.2:** Why does it make sense to combine those three programs? Clean Energy Transition is still small. Why didn't we fold it in too, and what would you do with it instead?

# ✅ Checkpoint 2: Seeing Relationships

## 5. 🆕 Scatterplot, Trend Line, and r
**functions:**
`geom_point()`: 🆕 One dot per row. `alpha` makes the dots see-through so crowded areas look darker.
`geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)`: 🆕 Draws the straight line of best fit.
`cor(x, y)`: 🆕 The correlation, r.

**logic steps:**
Plot `precipitation_mm` (x) against `temp_c` (y). Use `alpha = 0.3`.
Add a straight trend line.
Calculate r for the same two columns.

```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot(station_years, aes(x = precipitation_mm, y = temp_c)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#274873") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#B8842E", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Rainier stations tend to be cooler",
    x = "Yearly rainfall (mm)",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

cor(station_years$precipitation_mm, station_years$temp_c)
```

**Question 5.1:** Describe the scatterplot using the four questions from lecture: direction, strength, form, and oddballs.

**Question 5.2:** What is r? Is that weak, moderate, or strong?

## 6. Box Plus Dots

### 6.1 ✅ The Boxplot
**functions:**
`geom_boxplot()`: Same as Section 1, now one box per group.

```{r}
ggplot(station_years, aes(x = reorder(energy_source, precipitation_mm, FUN = median), y = precipitation_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#2a9d8f", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "Rainfall by Energy Source", x = NULL, y = "Yearly rainfall (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 6.2 🆕 Add the Dots
**functions:**
`geom_jitter()`: 🆕 Like `geom_point()`, but nudges each dot a little sideways so they don't pile on top of each other.
`outlier.shape = NA`: 🆕 Stops the boxplot from drawing its own outlier dots, since the jitter already shows every point.

**logic steps:**
Copy your boxplot from 6.1. Add `outlier.shape = NA` inside `geom_boxplot()`.
Add a `geom_jitter()` layer with `width = 0.2` and `alpha = 0.3`.

```{r}
ggplot(station_years, aes(x = reorder(energy_source, precipitation_mm, FUN = median), y = precipitation_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#2a9d8f", alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3, color = "#274873") +
  labs(title = "Rainfall by Energy Source", x = NULL, y = "Yearly rainfall (mm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 6.1:** What do the dots show that the box alone hid? (Hint: look at Wind.)

## 7. 🆕 Category vs. Category: Count Heatmap
**functions:**
`count(a, b)`: Counts every combination of two columns (Lab 3).
`factor(levels = )`: Sets the order Low → Medium → High (Lab 2).
`geom_tile()`: 🆕 Draws a grid of colored squares.
`geom_text()`: 🆕 Writes a label on each square.
`scale_fill_viridis_c()`: 🆕 Colorblind-safe palette for numbers.

**logic steps:**
Count `energy_source` by `climate_risk_level`.
Make `climate_risk_level` an ordered factor so it reads Low → Medium → High.
Draw a tile per combination, filled by the count, with the count written on top.

```{r}
station_years %>%
  count(energy_source, climate_risk_level) %>%
  mutate(climate_risk_level = factor(climate_risk_level, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = climate_risk_level, y = energy_source, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", size = 5) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Station-years") +
  labs(title = "Energy Source by Climate Risk Level", x = "Climate risk level", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 7.1:** Which combination is the most common? Does anything about it surprise you, given what you learned about Solar stations in Section 2?

## 8. Change Over Time

### 8.1 ✅ The Average Line
**functions:**
`group_by()` + `summarize()`, `geom_line()`: Lab 2 and Lab 3.

```{r}
co2_by_year <- station_years %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(avg_co2 = mean(co2_ppm))

ggplot(co2_by_year, aes(x = year, y = avg_co2)) +
  geom_line(color = "#274873", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#274873", size = 2.5) +
  labs(title = "Average CO2 by Year", x = NULL, y = "Average CO2 (ppm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 8.2 🆕 Annotate It
**functions:**
`annotate("text", x =, y =, label =)`: 🆕 Writes your own text anywhere on the chart.
`paste0()`: Glues text and numbers together into one label.

**logic steps:**
Calculate `co2_rise`: the last year's average minus the first year's.
Copy the chart from 8.1. Add an `annotate()` layer in the empty top-left corner that says how much CO2 rose.
Change the title so it states the takeaway.

```{r}
co2_rise <- max(co2_by_year$avg_co2) - min(co2_by_year$avg_co2)

ggplot(co2_by_year, aes(x = year, y = avg_co2)) +
  geom_line(color = "#274873", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#274873", size = 2.5) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 2016, y = 417, hjust = 0, size = 5, color = "#B8842E",
    label = paste0("+", round(co2_rise, 1), " ppm in 6 years")
  ) +
  labs(title = "CO2 rose every single year", x = NULL, y = "Average CO2 (ppm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 8.3 🆕 Highlight One Station
**functions:**
`aes(group = )`: 🆕 Tells `geom_line()` to draw one separate line per station.
`filter()`: Keeps one station's rows (Lab 1).
Two `geom_line()` layers: 🆕 The second layer uses its own `data =`, so it draws on top of the first.

**logic steps:**
Draw every station's `temp_c` over `year` as a thin gray line, one line per `location`.
Add a second `geom_line()` that uses only Lakevale's rows, in a bold color.
Label Lakevale with `annotate()`.

```{r}
lakevale <- station_years %>% filter(location == "Lakevale")

ggplot(station_years, aes(x = year, y = temp_c, group = location)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey85") +
  geom_line(data = lakevale, color = "#B8842E", linewidth = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 2022.1, y = max(lakevale$temp_c), hjust = 0, color = "#B8842E",
           label = "Lakevale") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(2016, 2023)) +
  labs(
    title = "Lakevale warmed faster than any other station",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 8.1:** What does the highlight chart show that a single average line would hide?

# ✅ Checkpoint 3: Seeing What's Hidden, and Telling the Story

## 9. The 3°C Mystery

### 9.1 🆕 Color by a Third Variable
**functions:**
`aes(color = )`: 🆕 Colors each dot by a category.
`scale_color_manual()`: 🆕 Picks the colors yourself.

**logic steps:**
Copy your scatterplot from Section 5 (without the trend line).
Color the dots by `funded`, using teal for Funded and gold for Not funded.

```{r}
ggplot(station_years, aes(x = precipitation_mm, y = temp_c, color = funded)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Funded" = "#2a9d8f", "Not funded" = "#B8842E")) +
  labs(
    title = "Funded station-years cluster on the rainy side",
    x = "Yearly rainfall (mm)",
    y = "Temperature (°C)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question 9.1:** Where do the teal (Funded) dots pile up? What does that suggest about the 3°C gap from Lab 4?

### 9.2 ✅ Compare Within Rain Bands
**functions:**
`case_when()`, `group_by()`, `summarize()`: Labs 2 to 4.

**logic steps:**
First, the overall gap (same as Lab 4).
Then split every station-year into a Dry, Medium, or Wet band, and compare Funded vs. Not funded inside each band.

```{r}
# The overall gap
station_years %>%
  group_by(funded) %>%
  summarize(avg_temp = mean(temp_c), n = n())

# The gap inside each rain band
station_years %>%
  mutate(rain_band = case_when(
    precipitation_mm < 500 ~ "1. Dry",      # under 500 mm
    precipitation_mm < 1000 ~ "2. Medium",  # 500 to 1000 mm
    TRUE ~ "3. Wet"                         # over 1000 mm
  )) %>%
  group_by(rain_band, funded) %>%
  summarize(avg_temp = mean(temp_c), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = funded, values_from = c(avg_temp, n))
```

**Question 9.2:** What happens to the 3°C gap inside each rain band?

## 10. 🆕 The Hydro Flip
**functions:**
`facet_wrap(~ group)`: One small chart per group (Lab 3).
`cor()` inside `summarize()`: 🆕 One r per group.

**logic steps:**
Copy your Section 5 chart (dots + trend line). Add `facet_wrap(~ energy_source)`.
Then calculate r for each energy source with `group_by()` + `summarize()`.

```{r, message=FALSE}
ggplot(station_years, aes(x = precipitation_mm, y = temp_c)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#274873") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#B8842E", linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ energy_source) +
  labs(
    title = "Rain vs. Temperature, Split by Energy Source",
    x = "Yearly rainfall (mm)",
    y = "Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

station_years %>%
  group_by(energy_source) %>%
  summarize(r = cor(precipitation_mm, temp_c))
```

**Question 10.1:** Which panel goes the *opposite* direction from the overall chart in Section 5? Which one is basically flat?

## 11. 🆕 Find the Twins
**functions:**
`select()`: Keeps only the columns you list (Lab 3).
`cor(table)`: 🆕 Given a whole table of numbers, returns r for every pair at once (a correlation matrix).
`as.data.frame(as.table())`: 🆕 Turns the matrix into a long table with one row per pair, so ggplot can draw it.
`scale_fill_gradient2()`: 🆕 A color scale with a middle point: one color for negative, white for 0, another for positive.
`ggpairs()`: 🆕 A scatterplot for every pair, plus each variable's shape, in one picture (from `GGally`).

**logic steps:**
Select the six number columns from `towns`: `avg_rain`, `avg_temp`, `avg_co2`, `storms`, `grants_millions`, `n_grants`.
Compute the correlation matrix and reshape it to long form.
Draw a tile heatmap with the r value written on each tile.
Then draw `ggpairs()` on the same six columns.

```{r, message=FALSE}
town_numbers <- towns %>%
  select(avg_rain, avg_temp, avg_co2, storms, grants_millions, n_grants)

cor_matrix <- cor(town_numbers)
cor_long <- as.data.frame(as.table(cor_matrix))

ggplot(cor_long, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = Freq)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Freq, 2))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#274873", mid = "white", high = "#B8842E", midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1), name = "r") +
  labs(title = "Correlation Heatmap (one row per town)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

ggpairs(town_numbers)
```

**Question 11.1:** Which pair of variables are twins? What is their r?

**Question 11.2:** Next week we'll predict things with models. If you had to keep only one of the twins, which would you keep, and why?

## 12. 🆕 Bubble Chart, Then Make It Interactive
**functions:**
`aes(size = )`: 🆕 Sizes each dot by a number.
`aes(text = )`: 🆕 The label that shows up when you hover. ggplot ignores it, but `ggplotly()` uses it.
`ggplotly(chart, tooltip = "text")`: 🆕 Turns a ggplot into an interactive chart (from `plotly`).

**logic steps:**
Plot `towns`: `avg_rain` on x and `grants_millions` on y.
Size each bubble by `storms` and color it by `risk_level`.
Build a hover label with `paste0()`: town name, rain, grants, and storms. `"<br>"` starts a new line.
Save the chart as `bubble`, then hand it to `ggplotly()`.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
bubble <- ggplot(towns, aes(
  x = avg_rain,
  y = grants_millions,
  size = storms,
  color = risk_level,
  text = paste0(
    location,
    "<br>Rain: ", round(avg_rain), " mm",
    "<br>Grants: $", round(grants_millions, 1), "M",
    "<br>Storms: ", storms
  )
)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Low" = "#2a9d8f", "Medium" = "#B8842E", "High" = "#9b2226")) +
  labs(
    title = "Rainier towns get more grant money",
    x = "Average yearly rainfall (mm)",
    y = "Total grants ($ millions)",
    color = "Risk level",
    size = "Storms"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

ggplotly(bubble, tooltip = "text")
```

**Question 12.1:** Hover around the chart. Which town surprises you the most, and why?

## 13. 🆕 The Interactive Map
**functions:**
`borders("state")`: 🆕 Draws US state outlines (from `maps`).
`coord_fixed(1.3)`: 🆕 Locks the shape so the US doesn't look stretched.
`theme_void()`: 🆕 Removes the axes and grid, which a map doesn't need.

**logic steps:**
Start with `ggplot()` and add the state borders.
Add a `geom_point()` layer with `data = towns`: `longitude` on x, `latitude` on y, color by `avg_rain`, size by `grants_millions`. Add a hover label.
Save it as `grant_map` and pass it to `ggplotly()` with `tooltip = "text"`.

```{r, warning=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
grant_map <- ggplot() +
  borders("state", fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(
    data = towns,
    aes(
      x = longitude,
      y = latitude,
      color = avg_rain,
      size = grants_millions,
      text = paste0(
        location,
        "<br>Rain: ", round(avg_rain), " mm",
        "<br>Grants: $", round(grants_millions, 1), "M"
      )
    ),
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(direction = -1) +
  coord_fixed(1.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Where the Rain Falls, and Where the Money Goes",
    color = "Rain (mm)",
    size = "Grants ($M)"
  ) +
  theme_void()

ggplotly(grant_map, tooltip = "text")
```

**Question 13.1:** Where is most of the grant money going? Does it follow the rain?

## 14. 🆕 Save Your Favorite
**functions:**
`ggsave("file.png", chart, width =, height =)`: 🆕 Saves a ggplot as an image file. (It saves the regular version, not the interactive one.)

**logic steps:**
Save `bubble` as `my_favorite_chart.png`, 8 inches wide and 5 inches tall.

```{r, warning=FALSE}
ggsave("my_favorite_chart.png", bubble, width = 8, height = 5)
```
